title: TLS certificate is valid
what: The certificate is trusted, matches the host and is not expired.
why: Browsers block the site outright and every user sees a warning.

title: TLS certificate is not about to expire
what: More than 14 days remain on the certificate.
why: An expired certificate takes the site down for everyone at once.

title: HTTP redirects to HTTPS
what: A plain http:// request answers with a 301 or 308 to https://.
why: Without it, sessions and forms can be read on the wire.

title: Strict-Transport-Security header
what: HSTS is present with max-age of at least 6 months.
why: Stops downgrade attacks after the first visit.

title: Content-Security-Policy present
what: A CSP header exists on the HTML response.
why: It is the only control that limits what injected scripts can do.

title: CSP has frame-ancestors and form-action and no wildcard script-src
what: The policy names frame-ancestors, form-action, and does not allow scripts from everywhere.
why: A CSP with a wildcard script-src protects nothing.

title: Clickjacking protection
what: X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors is set.
why: Without it the site can be framed inside an attacker's page.

title: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
what: The nosniff header is present.
why: Stops browsers from guessing content types into executable ones.

title: Referrer-Policy set
what: A Referrer-Policy header is present.
why: Keeps URLs with tokens from leaking to third parties.

title: Permissions-Policy set
what: A Permissions-Policy header is present.
why: Turns off camera, microphone and location APIs the site never uses.

title: Cookies are Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
what: Every Set-Cookie on the HTML response carries the three flags where appropriate.
why: A session cookie without HttpOnly is one XSS away from theft.

title: No wildcard CORS with credentials
what: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is not * alongside Allow-Credentials true.
why: Any site on the internet could call the API as the signed-in user.

title: Server software not advertised
what: No Server or X-Powered-By header naming versions.
why: Version strings help attackers pick exploits.

title: No source maps served
what: First-party JavaScript does not reference a reachable .map file.
why: Source maps hand over the original code, comments and often keys.

title: No secret keys in client JavaScript
what: First-party bundles contain no secret-shaped strings: Stripe sk_, Supabase service_role, AWS, OpenAI, Anthropic, Twilio, SendGrid, Resend.
why: A secret key in the bundle is a full compromise of that service.

title: Supabase REST metadata not readable with the public key
what: If the page ships a Supabase URL and anon key, the REST root does not list tables to anonymous callers.
why: Table names are the map; the verified check reads the rows.

title: Firebase config present (rules unverified)
what: A Firebase web config is in the bundle; rules cannot be judged passively.
why: Open Firestore or Storage rules are the Firebase form of RLS off.

title: Production is not running on a Stripe test key
what: On a production domain the publishable key is pk_live, not pk_test.
why: Customers on a test key cannot pay, and nobody notices until launch day.

title: No builder leftovers
what: No dev-server hints, placeholder copy, builder badges or chat residue in the HTML.
why: Leftovers tell visitors and attackers the site was never reviewed.

title: No env files served by URL
what: /.env, /.env.local, /.env.production and .bak variants return 404.
why: One of these being a 200 is the most common total compromise.

title: No .git directory served
what: /.git/config and /.git/HEAD return 404.
why: A served .git lets anyone download the whole repository and its history.

title: Internal files return 404
what: README.md, CLAUDE.md, docs/ and scripts/ are not served.
why: Internal docs describe the system to anyone who asks.

title: Admin and API routes refuse anonymous requests
what: Routes found in the sitemap and bundle answer 401, 403 or 405 to an anonymous request, never data.
why: Client-side-only authorization is the Enrichlead failure.

title: Anonymous callers cannot read table rows
what: With the page's own anon key, every exposed table returns zero rows to an anonymous select.
why: RLS off is the cause of nearly every reported vibe-coded data leak.

title: Storage buckets are not listable
what: Supabase or Firebase storage does not list objects to anonymous callers.
why: Listable buckets leak uploads, IDs and documents.

title: Endpoints are rate limited
what: Ten rapid requests to one endpoint produce a 429 or equivalent.
why: Unmetered endpoints turn into runaway bills and brute force.

title: No secrets committed in the repository
what: A secret scan over the full history finds nothing live.
why: A committed secret is public even after the commit is deleted.

title: Ignore rules cover the whole env family
what: git check-ignore proves .env, .env.*, and *.bak* are ignored.
why: A rule that covers .env but not .env.local.bak has leaked every token at once.

title: Env example lists every variable the code reads
what: Every variable read in code appears in .env.example with a placeholder.
why: Missing variables are the first deploy-day failure.

title: Auth settings are closed by default
what: Signup matches intent, minimum password is 12 or more, OTP expiry and redirect allow-list are set, anonymous sign-ins off.
why: Auth provider settings are attack surface the code never shows.

title: Row level security is on and policies are correct
what: Every table has RLS enabled and no policy is USING (true) for anon.
why: A table with RLS on and a permissive policy is RLS off with extra steps.

title: Stripe webhook points at the live domain
what: A webhook endpoint exists for the production domain, is enabled, and subscribes to the checkout and payment events the code handles.
why: Without it payments succeed and nothing is delivered.

title: Hosting env values are clean and scoped
what: No value ends in a newline; production and preview values are scoped; no secret sits in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ name.
why: A trailing newline in a Stripe key fails every charge with a misleading error.

title: SPF record present and single
what: Exactly one SPF TXT record at the apex.
why: Two SPF records equal none; mail from the domain is unauthenticated.

title: DKIM record found
what: A DKIM record resolves for a common selector (resend, google, default, k1, selector1).
why: Without DKIM, transactional mail lands in spam.

title: DMARC policy published
what: _dmarc exists with a policy of quarantine or reject and a reporting address.
why: DMARC is what inbox providers check first in 2026.

title: MX records present
what: The domain can receive mail.
why: Reply addresses that bounce lose customers and break password resets.

title: Magic-link and receipt emails come from an authenticated domain
what: The sending domain implied by DKIM selectors or a Supabase default sender has SPF and DMARC.
why: Auth emails from an unauthenticated sender go to spam, and users cannot sign in.

title: Nameservers identified
what: The DNS provider is identified.
why: Context for the other checks.

title: DNSSEC enabled
what: The zone is signed.
why: Prevents cache-poisoning of the domain.

title: CAA record present
what: A CAA record limits which authorities can issue certificates.
why: Cheap protection against mis-issued certificates.

title: Domain not about to expire
what: More than 30 days remain on the registration.
why: An expired domain takes down the site, email and every login at once.

title: security.txt published
what: /.well-known/security.txt exists with a contact.
why: Researchers who find a hole need somewhere to send it.

title: Privacy and terms pages discoverable
what: Links to a privacy policy and terms are present on the home page and resolve.
why: Stripe, app stores and ad platforms require them; users expect them.

title: Title present and 30 to 60 characters
what: The home page title length is in range.
why: The title is the search result.

title: Meta description present and 70 to 155 characters
what: The description length is in range.
why: Controls the snippet under the title.

title: Self-referencing canonical
what: A canonical link points at the page itself.
why: Prevents duplicate-URL dilution.

title: Exactly one H1
what: The home page has one H1.
why: Headings are structure for crawlers and screen readers.

title: lang and viewport set
what: The html element has lang and a viewport meta exists.
why: Mobile rendering and accessibility depend on both.

title: Open Graph image resolves
what: og:image is absolute, returns 200 and is at least 1200 by 630.
why: Every share on every platform shows this image or a blank.

title: JSON-LD parses
what: Structured data blocks parse as JSON.
why: Broken JSON-LD is ignored silently.

title: robots.txt valid
what: /robots.txt returns 200 text/plain and names the sitemap.
why: A missing or broken robots file blocks or mis-directs crawlers.

title: Sitemap present and healthy
what: /sitemap.xml returns 200 and a sample of its URLs return 200.
why: Sitemaps with dead URLs waste crawl budget and signal neglect.

title: Missing pages return 404
what: A random path returns HTTP 404 with the site's own page, not 200.
why: A soft 404 lets search engines index garbage and hides real breakage.

title: Favicon present
what: A favicon resolves.
why: A missing favicon is the first sign of an unfinished site.

title: No mixed content
what: No http:// assets on the https page.
why: Browsers block or warn, and the lock icon disappears.

title: No broken links on the home page
what: Internal links on the home page resolve.
why: Dead links on page one lose trust and crawl budget.

title: llms.txt present
what: /llms.txt exists.
why: Low-cost hint for AI crawlers; hygiene, not strategy.

title: AI crawler policy is deliberate
what: robots.txt states a choice for GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended.
why: Being cited by answer engines starts with letting them in on purpose.

title: Analytics installed
what: GA4, Plausible, PostHog, Fathom or equivalent is loaded.
why: Launching without measurement means never knowing what worked.

title: Consent mechanism where required
what: A consent control exists if the site targets regions that require one.
why: Required for EU and UK visitors when tracking is on.

title: Time to first byte under 800 ms
what: The HTML response starts within 800 ms.
why: Slow origins hurt ranking and conversion.

title: Home page under 2 MB
what: Total transfer for the home page is under 2 MB.
why: Weight is the mobile experience.

title: Largest image under 300 KB
what: No image on the home page exceeds 300 KB.
why: One unoptimized hero image is usually half the page.

title: Few render-blocking resources
what: Fewer than four blocking scripts or stylesheets in the head.
why: Blocking resources delay first paint.
